label: Problem set 8
title: Problem set 8: Controlled-current techniques
summary: Practice with chronopotentiometry: the Sand equation, transition times, current reversal and the effect of iR drop.

intro.text: Controlled-current (chronopotentiometric) methods force a constant current and follow the potential. The transition time follows the Sand equation i t^(1/2) = nFAD^(1/2)pi^(1/2)C/2.
The transition time falls as 1/i^2, and a large forced current magnifies any uncompensated-resistance iR drop in the measured potential.

blocks.text: Controlled-current (chronopotentiometric) methods force a constant current and follow the potential. The transition time follows the Sand equation i t^(1/2) = nFAD^(1/2)pi^(1/2)C/2.
The transition time falls as 1/i^2, and a large forced current magnifies any uncompensated-resistance iR drop in the measured potential.

blocks.title: Transition time from the Sand equation

questions.question: Use the Sand equation i t^(1/2) = nFAD^(1/2)pi^(1/2)C/2 to find the transition time t (s) for n = 1, A = 1.0 cm2, D = 1.0e-5 cm2/s, C = 1.0e-6 mol/cm3 and i = 1.0e-3 A.

The Sand equation gives the transition time as proportional to 1/i^2. If the current is quadrupled, by what fraction of its original value does the transition time change? (Answer as a fraction, e.g. 0.25.)
questions.explanation: t scales with 1/i^2, so quadrupling i divides t by 16, giving 1/16 = 0.0625.

questions.question: Chronopotentiometry records:
options: Potential as a function of time under a constant applied current
Current as a function of time under a constant potential
Impedance against frequency
Mass against charge
questions.explanation: In a constant-current experiment the potential is followed with time; it jumps sharply at the transition time when the reactant at the surface is exhausted.

questions.question: The transition time in chronopotentiometry is the time at which the surface concentration of the reactant reaches zero.
questions.explanation: Up to the transition time the reactant still arrives by diffusion; once the surface is depleted the potential must swing to a new reaction, giving the characteristic jump.

questions.question: A practical drawback of controlled-current methods at large currents is that:
options: The iR drop in solution can distort the measured potential
No current flows
The solution freezes
The electrode area changes to zero
questions.explanation: Because a fixed current is forced through the cell, an uncompensated resistance can consume part of the applied voltage as iR drop and distort the potential-time curve, especially at high current.

questions.question: Reversing the current part-way through a chronopotentiometric experiment lets the product of the first step be examined.
questions.explanation: Current reversal oxidises or reduces whatever was produced in the forward step, and the reverse transition time gives information about the product and its reactions.

questions.question: Which statements about chronopotentiometry are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A constant current is applied
The potential-time curve shows a sharp change at the transition time
The transition time increases with concentration
The potential stays constant after the transition time
questions.explanation: A constant current is applied, the potential jumps at the transition time, and a higher concentration lengthens that transition time. After the transition the potential shifts to a new reaction rather than staying constant.

questions.question: For diffusion-controlled chronopotentiometry the product i t^(1/2) is a constant. If i = 1.0 mA gives t = 4.0 s, what is i t^(1/2) in mA s^(1/2)?
In chronopotentiometry the potential before the transition time is determined by the Nernst equation applied at the electrode surface.
questions.explanation: As the surface concentration of the reactant falls, the potential follows the Nernst equation until the surface is depleted at the transition time.

questions.question: The transition time is proportional to 1/i^2. If t = 4.0 s at i = 1.0 mA, what is t in seconds when the current is doubled to 2.0 mA?
questions.explanation: Doubling i divides t by 4, so t = 4.0/4 = 1.0 s.

questions.question: For diffusion-controlled chronopotentiometry the product i t^(1/2) is constant. If i = 1.0 mA gives t = 4.0 s, what is i t^(1/2) in mA s^(1/2)?
The main experimental difficulty of controlled-current methods at high current is:
options: The uncompensated-resistance iR drop distorting the measured potential
The absence of any current
The reference electrode dissolving
The solution becoming transparent
questions.explanation: A large forced current through an uncompensated resistance consumes voltage as iR drop, which distorts the measured potential-time curve unless it is compensated.

questions.question: After the transition time the electrode potential shifts to a new electrode reaction.
questions.explanation: Once the original reactant is exhausted at the surface, the potential moves to whatever reaction can now carry the fixed current.

questions.question: Which are true of the Sand equation? Select all that apply.
options: It relates current and transition time
It contains the diffusion coefficient and concentration
It predicts t proportional to 1/i^2
It contains the electrode resistance
questions.explanation: The Sand equation links i and t through D and C and predicts t proportional to 1/i^2. It does not contain the electrode resistance.
